title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is rolling out a new interface design that looks sleek and modern but no longer works properly with screen readers. The manager uses external business pressures, competitive arguments, and organizational constraints to justify the accessibility problems despite user impact concerns.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Thanks for bringing this up. I understand there might be some minor navigation hiccups with screen readers, but let's keep this in perspective - most of our user interactions happen through the main interface paths which are working fine. The form is functional, it's just that some users might need to take a slightly different approach to complete their updates.

user_choices.choice: If I were a screen reader user, I'd be completely unable to update my profile information.
user_choices.justification: Adopts user perspective to highlight their experience

user_choices.choice: You're right that it's still technically functional, just with a different user experience.
user_choices.justification: Concedes to manager's minimization of the issue

user_choices.choice: I understand the technical complexity, but we can't ship something that completely excludes disabled users.

user_choices.choice: Minor navigation issues are probably acceptable if the core functionality works.
user_choices.justification: Draws broad conclusion from limited perspective

step_2.text: I appreciate your concern for different user groups, but we need to prioritize realistically. Our analytics show that users requiring screen readers represent less than 1% of our total user base. While I don't want to ignore them completely, we have to balance our development resources against features that will benefit the vast majority of our users.

user_choices.justification: Accepts numerical minimization of user impact

user_choices.justification: Justifies decisions based on majority preference

shutdown_2.text: Exactly, I'm glad you understand the bigger picture here. Different user experiences aren't necessarily broken experiences - they're just alternative pathways. Let's focus our energy on the features that will have the broadest positive impact for our user community.

user_choices.choice: Wait, alternative pathways still need to be actually functional for screen reader users.

user_choices.choice: Broader impact initiatives do seem like the logical priority.

step_3.text: I hear what you're saying, but let's look at this objectively. Our accessibility compliance score is already 85%, which puts us well above industry average. The screen reader issue affects a very specific subset of that already small 1% user group. While I understand it's frustrating for those few users, we have to weigh this against more pressing issues that impact thousands of users daily.

user_choices.choice: 85% compliance means we're doing better than most companies, so this isn't urgent.

bad_ending.text: The manager proceeds with the original plan, treating screen reader compatibility as a minor inconvenience rather than a blocking issue. The project ships with accessibility problems minimized as 'alternative user pathways' while fundamental usability remains broken.
bad_ending.title: Issue Minimized
bad_ending.learning: Diluter managers often use statistics and relative impact arguments to make serious accessibility issues seem less important. Effective advocacy requires concrete evidence and reframing the issue's true scope.

mid_ending.text: The manager agrees to some basic accessibility improvements but frames them as enhancements rather than critical fixes. Some issues are addressed but the underlying minimization of accessibility importance remains.
mid_ending.title: Partial Recognition
mid_ending.learning: Partial progress with diluter managers often comes with continued minimization of the issue's importance. Sustained advocacy is needed to achieve recognition of accessibility as essential functionality.

good_ending.text: The manager recognizes that accessibility isn't just about numbers but about fundamental usability. The screen reader issues are properly addressed and framed as core functionality rather than edge cases.
good_ending.title: Perspective Shift
good_ending.learning: Success with diluter managers requires shifting their focus from statistics to user impact, demonstrating that accessibility issues represent genuine barriers rather than minor inconveniences.
